items.title: Two equal pours of wine and water never separate again
items.claim: Pour a cup of wine into a barrel of water. Stir. Now pour a cup of the mixture back into the wine. Compared to the original: is there more wine in the water-barrel, or more water in the wine-barrel?

options.text: More wine in water (because it was poured first)
More water in wine (because the second cup contained mixture, not pure water)
Equal — by conservation of volume, the amount of wine missing from the wine barrel exactly equals the amount of water now in the wine barrel
Cannot be determined without more information

items.reveal:
Both barrels started with their own volume (V wine and V water). After two exchanges of one cup each, the volumes are still V wine and V water (volume is conserved in each barrel).

Let's say the wine barrel now contains x amount of water and (V - x) wine. The wine barrel's contents totals V — so by mass balance, V - (V - x) = x amount of wine has LEFT the wine barrel. Where did it go? It is now in the water barrel.

So: water in wine barrel = x; wine in water barrel = x. Always equal — regardless of how messy the mixing was, or whether the cups were exact, or how much you stirred.

This is a classic riddle dating to mediaeval mathematics. People reach for arithmetic and get tangled in fractions. A two-line conservation argument settles it without computation.

Generalisation: for ANY pair of equal-volume transfers (cup A to barrel B, then equal-volume cup B' to barrel A), the impurity in each ends up equal. The riddle is independent of mixing details.

Lesson for problem-solving: pure-conservation arguments often resolve mixing problems faster than direct calculation. The same idea underlies many chemistry-stoichiometry problems and the 'rule of alligation' in pharmacy.
items.why: Mixing problems feel like they need detailed arithmetic. Conservation reasoning bypasses the arithmetic entirely — and is more reliable, because it's robust to the details you don't know.

items.title: The angles of a triangle on a globe don't add to 180 degrees
items.claim: Draw a triangle from the North Pole to the equator at 0 degrees longitude, along the equator to 90 degrees longitude, and back to the North Pole. All three angles are 90 degrees. Total: 270.
items.prompt: How can a triangle have 270 degrees?

options.text: On a curved surface, the angle sum exceeds 180 by an amount proportional to the area enclosed (spherical excess); on a sphere of radius R, sum = 180 + (area / R^2) in radians times 180/pi

items.reveal:
On a flat Euclidean plane, the angles of a triangle sum to exactly 180 degrees.

On a sphere (positive curvature), the sum is more than 180. The excess is proportional to the area: Sum - 180 = (Area / R^2) * (180/pi) for a sphere of radius R. The example triangle (pole-equator-equator-pole) covers 1/8 of the Earth's surface — area ~ 6.4 * 10^7 square km — and has excess 90 degrees.

On a hyperbolic plane (negative curvature), the sum is LESS than 180. The deficit is proportional to area.

This is the deepest test of non-Euclidean geometry: by measuring the angle sum of a triangle, you can tell what kind of space you're in.

Gauss attempted to measure the angle sum of a triangle formed by three mountain peaks (Hohenhagen, Brocken, Inselsberg) in 1820s to test whether space itself is Euclidean. He found no measurable deviation from 180, given his instruments' precision.

General relativity: mass curves space-time. Light follows geodesics through curved space-time. Two photons from a distant source, passing on either side of the Sun, converge (negative curvature in tested region's measurement frame). Detected during the 1919 solar eclipse — confirmation of Einstein.
items.why: Triangles seem to obviously sum to 180. They do on flat surfaces. Real Earth navigation, general relativity, and modern cosmology all use non-Euclidean geometry where triangle sums are observably different.

items.title: The most important open problem in mathematics
items.claim: Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2. The conjecture controls the distribution of primes among integers. Proving (or disproving) it has been unsolved for 165 years.
items.prompt: Why do we care about complex zeros of a strange function?

options.text: The distribution of prime numbers is encoded in the zeros of the Riemann zeta function — proving the Riemann hypothesis would establish a vast number of theorems in number theory that are currently conditional on it
It tells us the value of zeta at integer points
It's part of the definition of pi

items.reveal:
Riemann's only paper on number theory (1859) defined the analytic continuation of the zeta function and noted that the function has 'trivial zeros' at -2, -4, -6, ... and other 'non-trivial zeros' in the strip 0 less than Re(s) less than 1. He conjectured all non-trivial zeros lie exactly on Re(s) = 1/2.

The Prime Number Theorem (Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin, 1896) says the count of primes up to x is asymptotically x / ln x. The Riemann hypothesis would tighten the error term enormously.

Thousands of theorems in modern number theory are stated 'assuming RH'. A proof would make them unconditional. Conversely, a disproof would force major rewrites.

The first 10 trillion non-trivial zeros have all been computed and verified to lie on Re(s) = 1/2 (Gourdon, 2004). This doesn't prove the hypothesis.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists it as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1,000,000 reward. So far, only Poincaré (Perelman, 2003) has been solved.
items.why: Primes look like a chaotic distribution. The Riemann hypothesis says they have hidden, beautiful regularity controlled by complex analysis — and 165 years of effort haven't proved or disproved it.
